cards.q: Distinguish public international law from private international law and from EU law. Give one example of a rule from each field. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Public international law governs relations between subjects of international law (above all states and international organizations); private international law is domestic conflict-of-laws law for private cross-border relations; EU law is an autonomous supranational order sui generis.
• Public international law (PIL): the rules governing the rights and obligations of subjects of international law in matters that do not belong exclusively to the internal law of one state. It is defined by its subjects (who bears rights and duties), not by a cross-border subject-matter. Example: prohibition of the use of force (Art 2(4) UN Charter), pacta sunt servanda (Art 26 VCLT), state immunity.
• Private international law (conflict of laws): rules deciding which national law applies and which court has jurisdiction in a private relationship with a foreign element (e.g. a contract between a Czech and an Austrian company). It is part of each state's domestic law (e.g. the Austrian IPR-Gesetz), even where harmonised by treaties or EU regulations (Rome I). The parties are private persons, not subjects of PIL.
• EU law: created by treaties between states, but an autonomous legal order with its own institutions, sources and court, direct effect and primacy in the member states (Van Gend en Loos, Costa/ENEL) — therefore not treated as ordinary international law.
• Test: who is bound and whose relations are governed? A cross-border element alone does not make a rule PIL.
Memorise: PIL = subjects (states/IOs) · private IL = which national law for private persons (domestic law) · EU law = sui generis (direct effect, primacy).

cards.q: In a seminar Lena argues: "Only states are subjects of international law. The United Nations, the ICRC, the Holy See and the Sovereign Order of Malta are just influential bodies, like Greenpeace or Amnesty International. And individuals can never have rights or duties under international law." Assess Lena's statement. Explain what international legal personality means and distinguish the different kinds of subjects. (5 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Lena is wrong — states are the only original, full and sovereign subjects, but international organizations, the ICRC, the Holy See, the Order of Malta and (partially) individuals also have international legal personality; NGOs such as Greenpeace or Amnesty have none.
• International legal personality = capacity to be a bearer of rights and obligations under international law (and to assert them: claims, treaties, diplomatic relations). It is graded, not all-or-nothing — subjects are not necessarily identical in nature or in the extent of their rights (Reparation for Injuries, ICJ 1949).
• States: original personality (derived from no one), full and the only sovereign subjects (population, territory, effective government, capacity to enter into relations — Montevideo Convention 1933).
• International organizations (e.g. the UN): derived personality — created by states through a founding treaty and limited to their functions; the UN is an international person, but not a state (Reparation for Injuries 1949).
• Sui generis subjects recognised by states: the Holy See (the subject; the Vatican City State is the territory — concordats, diplomatic relations); the Sovereign Order of Malta (no territory, yet diplomatic relations and treaties with many states — territory is a condition of statehood, not of personality); the ICRC (a private association under Swiss law with limited personality from the functions entrusted to it by the Geneva Conventions 1949 and Additional Protocols 1977).
• Individuals and corporations: partial personality — rights under human rights treaties (individual complaints, e.g. ECHR), duties under international criminal law (ICC Statute), investor rights under investment treaties. Also insurgents and national liberation movements (limited).
• NGOs: no personality, however influential — they are not established by agreement between states (ECOSOC Res 288 B (X) 1950) and have only consultative status (Art 71 UN Charter). Influence is not personality.
Memorise: states = original + full + sovereign · IOs = created, functional · Holy See / Malta / ICRC = recognised, sui generis · individuals = partial · NGOs = none.

cards.q: The newly elected president of Valdoria declares: "Valdoria is a sovereign state. Sovereignty means that no rule binds us unless our parliament has adopted it, and we can free ourselves from any international obligation at any time by a simple declaration." Assess the statement with reference to the different conceptions of sovereignty. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The president relies on the outdated absolute conception; under the prevailing relative conception Valdoria is subject to no other state, but it is bound by international law.
• Absolute sovereignty (Hegel: international law as mere "external state law"): a state could withdraw from any rule unilaterally — international law would then not be law at all. Rejected today.
• Relative sovereignty (prevailing): no state is subject to another state (par in parem non habet imperium; sovereign equality, Art 2(1) UN Charter), but all states are subject to international law. Sovereignty = independence, i.e. the exclusive right to exercise state functions on one's territory (Island of Palmas 1928) — within the limits of international law.
• Internal sovereignty (supreme authority over persons and things on the territory, today qualified by human rights and R2P) vs external sovereignty (independence and formal equality, "one state, one vote").
• Application: (1) customary law binds Valdoria without any act of its parliament (tacit, general consent; only a persistent objector escapes a new rule; ius cogens binds all); (2) a treaty binds once consent has been given (Art 26 VCLT), internal law is no excuse (Art 27 VCLT), and withdrawal is possible only under the treaty's terms or the VCLT (Arts 54, 56 — e.g. 12 months' notice), not by a simple declaration with immediate effect.
Memorise: absolute (Hegel) rejected · relative: subject to no STATE, but to international LAW · Art 2(1) Charter · Island of Palmas · Arts 26, 27, 56 VCLT.

cards.q: A cargo ship flying the flag of Marelia collides on the high seas with a fishing vessel of Toskania; several Toskanian fishermen die. When the Marelian officer on watch later arrives in a Toskanian port, Toskania arrests and prosecutes him. Marelia argues that Toskania would need a rule of international law permitting such jurisdiction. Explain the "Lotus principle" and assess whether the prosecution would have been lawful in 1927 and whether it is lawful today. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Under the Lotus principle states are free unless a prohibitive rule exists, so in 1927 the prosecution was not unlawful; today Art 97 UNCLOS reserves penal proceedings for high-seas collisions to the flag state or the state of nationality, so Toskania's prosecution would be unlawful.
• Lotus (PCIJ 1927, France v Turkey, decided by the President's casting vote): international law does not lay down a general prohibition on extending laws and jurisdiction to persons and acts outside the territory; it leaves states a wide measure of discretion, limited only by prohibitive rules. Restrictions upon the independence of states cannot be presumed.
• Consequence: "what is not prohibited is permitted" — the state alleging a prohibition bears the burden of proving the prohibitive rule (treaty or custom). This is why proving custom matters.
• 1927: France could not prove a customary rule of exclusive flag-state jurisdiction; the effects on the Turkish ship were treated like effects on Turkish territory → no violation by Turkey.
• Today: the result has been reversed — Art 11 High Seas Convention 1958, now Art 97(1) UNCLOS: penal proceedings only before the flag state or the state of which the accused is a national. Toskania (neither) would violate that rule.
• The principle survives as a residual approach (Kosovo AO 2010: no prohibition of declarations of independence), but is criticised as too state-centric.
Memorise: Lotus 1927 = freedom unless prohibited; burden on whoever alleges the prohibition · collisions now Art 97 UNCLOS · echoed in Kosovo AO 2010.

cards.q: Explain the theories of monism and dualism on the relationship between international law and domestic law. How does the Austrian Federal Constitution (B-VG) incorporate customary international law and treaties into Austrian law? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Dualism sees two separate legal orders (international rules must be transformed), monism one unified order (usually with primacy of international law); Austria incorporates custom automatically under Art 9(1) B-VG, while treaties need parliamentary approval under Art 50 B-VG and may be subject to an Erfüllungsvorbehalt.
• Dualism (Triepel, Anzilotti): international and domestic law are separate orders with different subjects and sources; an international rule applies domestically only after transformation by a domestic act.
• Monism (Kelsen, Verdross — the Vienna School): one single legal order. Radical monism with primacy of international law: conflicting domestic law is void; moderate monism: conflicting domestic law remains valid domestically, but applying it engages the state's international responsibility.
• International law's own view: it leaves the method of implementation to each state, but internal law never justifies a breach (Art 27 VCLT; Art 3 ARSIWA).
• Austria — custom: Art 9(1) B-VG: "the generally recognised rules of international law are regarded as integral parts of federal law" → general customary law applies automatically, without any act of transformation (lecture examples: state immunity, immunity of foreign officials, state succession).
• Austria — treaties: political and law-amending or law-supplementing treaties require approval by the National Council under Art 50 B-VG (plus the Federal Council where Länder competences are affected); the Federal President concludes/ratifies them (Art 65 B-VG); publication in the Federal Law Gazette (BGBl III). They are then applicable domestically unless the National Council resolves under Art 50(2) B-VG that the treaty is to be fulfilled by statutes (Erfüllungsvorbehalt → not directly applicable; comparable to non-self-executing). Internationally the treaty binds Austria either way.
Memorise: dualism = 2 orders + transformation · monism = 1 order (Kelsen) · AT: custom → Art 9(1) B-VG automatic · treaty → Art 50 approval + Art 65 ratification + BGBl · Erfüllungsvorbehalt = no direct application.

cards.q: An Austrian citizen sues State Norvania before a Vienna court for damages, because Norvanian police officers mistreated him during a demonstration in Norvania's capital. He argues that no Austrian statute grants immunity to foreign states, so the Austrian court must hear the case. Is he right? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No — state immunity is a rule of customary international law, which forms part of Austrian federal law automatically under Art 9(1) B-VG, so the court must apply it even without a statute and decline jurisdiction.
• Art 9(1) B-VG: the generally recognised rules of international law (general custom) are integral parts of federal law — no implementing statute is needed; Austrian courts apply them directly.
• State immunity (par in parem non habet imperium) is such a rule. Under the restrictive doctrine a state enjoys immunity for sovereign acts (acta iure imperii), not for commercial acts (acta iure gestionis) (ICJ, Jurisdictional Immunities, Germany v Italy 2012).
• Police conduct in Norvania is a typical sovereign act; even allegations of serious human rights violations do not remove immunity under current custom (Germany v Italy 2012). → The claim must be dismissed for lack of jurisdiction unless Norvania waives its immunity.
Memorise: custom in Austria = Art 9(1) B-VG, automatic · immunity for acta iure imperii only · Germany v Italy 2012.

cards.q: Name and briefly explain the sources of international law listed in Article 38(1) of the ICJ Statute. Which sources are not listed there, and what is the status of judicial decisions and teachings? (5 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Art 38(1)(a)–(c) lists the formal sources — treaties, custom and general principles of law; (d) judicial decisions and teachings are only subsidiary means; binding decisions of international organizations and unilateral acts are sources not mentioned in Art 38.
• (a) International conventions, general or particular, establishing rules expressly recognised by the contesting states: treaties, based on express consent, binding only the parties (pacta tertiis, Art 34 VCLT).
• (b) International custom, as evidence of a general practice accepted as law: state practice + opinio iuris; unwritten; binds all states except persistent objectors.
• (c) General principles of law recognised by "civilized nations" (today: the principal legal systems of the world), e.g. good faith, estoppel, res judicata; gap filling so that a court need not declare a non liquet.
• (d) Judicial decisions and the teachings of the most highly qualified publicists as subsidiary means for the determination of rules of law, "subject to Art 59" (a decision binds only the parties and only in that case) → no stare decisis; they help to find the law but do not create it.
• Not listed (the text dates from the 1920 PCIJ Statute): binding decisions of international organizations, e.g. Security Council resolutions under Chapter VII (Art 25 Charter; SC Res 1373 (2001): "decides that all States shall"); unilateral acts of states (Nuclear Tests 1974).
• Soft law (e.g. UDHR 1948, non-binding GA resolutions) is not a source at all — it lies below the "normative threshold", though it can influence law.
• The order in Art 38 is not a hierarchy; only ius cogens ranks above the other sources.
Memorise: Art 38(1): a treaties · b custom · c GPL · d subsidiary means (decisions + teachings, Art 59) · plus IO decisions + unilateral acts · soft law is no source.

cards.q: Do you agree with the following statement? Give reasons. "Because treaties are listed first in Article 38(1) of the ICJ Statute, a treaty always prevails over a conflicting rule of customary international law." (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No — the sources of international law are of equal rank; conflicts are resolved by lex specialis and lex posterior, and the only true hierarchy is ius cogens (plus the priority rule of Art 103 UN Charter).
• Art 38(1) is a list, not a ranking: treaties, custom, general principles, unilateral acts and binding IO decisions stand on the same level. A treaty may derogate from custom between its parties, and later custom may modify a treaty.
• Conflict rules: lex specialis derogat legi generali (the more specific rule prevails — e.g. a bilateral treaty over general custom between the same states); lex posterior derogat legi priori (the later rule prevails; for successive treaties Art 30(3) VCLT); but lex posterior generalis non derogat legi priori speciali.
• Exceptions with a hierarchy: ius cogens prevails over any conflicting treaty or custom — a conflicting treaty is void (Arts 53, 64 VCLT); Art 103 UN Charter: Charter obligations prevail over obligations under any other international agreement.
• Hence a treaty prevails over custom only where it is the more specific or the later rule — and never over ius cogens.
Memorise: no hierarchy of sources · lex specialis / lex posterior · above all: ius cogens · Art 103 Charter priority.

cards.q: In 1995 Arvenia and Belloria concluded a bilateral treaty allowing each other's fishing vessels to fish up to 20 nautical miles from the other's coast. Assume that in the 2010s a general customary rule emerged allowing coastal states to reserve fishing within 30 nautical miles exclusively to their own nationals. Belloria now invokes the new custom and bans Arvenian vessels from its 30-mile zone. Arvenia protests. Which rule prevails? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The bilateral treaty prevails: as the special rule between the two states it is not displaced by a later general custom, so Belloria's ban breaches the treaty.
• No hierarchy between treaty and custom; conflicts are solved by conflict rules. Lex posterior would favour the custom, but lex posterior generalis non derogat legi priori speciali: a later general rule does not in principle override an earlier special rule agreed between particular states.
• Custom is dispositive (not ius cogens): states may contract out of it inter se. The new custom creates an entitlement a coastal state may use, not a prohibition of treaties granting access.
• Application: the 1995 treaty is lex specialis between Arvenia and Belloria and remains in force (Art 26 VCLT). Belloria may rely on the new custom against third states, but not against Arvenia, unless both parties agreed — expressly or by concordant later conduct — to set the treaty rule aside; Arvenia's protest excludes this.
• Belloria's options: terminate or withdraw under the treaty's terms or the VCLT (Arts 54, 56); fundamental change of circumstances (Art 62) would be hard to argue.
Memorise: special earlier treaty beats later general custom (lex posterior generalis non derogat legi priori speciali) · custom is dispositive · protest blocks modification.

cards.q: States Karvia and Lomeria conclude a secret treaty in which they agree to invade their neighbour State Cordia jointly and to divide its territory between them. Is the treaty valid? Explain the concept of ius cogens, how peremptory norms arise and what legal effects they have. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The treaty is void from the outset under Art 53 VCLT, because it conflicts with a peremptory norm — the prohibition of aggression.
• Definition (Art 53 VCLT): a peremptory norm of general international law is a norm accepted and recognised by the international community of states as a whole as a norm from which no derogation is permitted and which can be modified only by a subsequent norm of general international law having the same character.
• Formation: usually on the basis of custom; "double acceptance" — the rule must be general international law AND be accepted by the community of states as a whole (a very large majority, not unanimity) as non-derogable.
• Examples: prohibition of aggression, genocide, slavery, torture, racial discrimination and apartheid, crimes against humanity, basic rules of IHL, right of self-determination.
• Effects: treaty conflicting at the time of conclusion is void in its entirety (Art 53, no severability Art 44(5)); a new peremptory norm makes an existing conflicting treaty void and terminate (Art 64); the consequences must be eliminated (Art 71); disputes can go to the ICJ (Art 66(a)). No persistent objector; no justification of a breach by circumstances precluding wrongfulness (Art 26 ARSIWA); serious breaches oblige all states to cooperate to end them and not to recognise the resulting situation (Arts 40–41 ARSIWA).
• Application: an agreement to invade and partition Cordia violates the prohibition of the use of force/aggression (Art 2(4) Charter, custom, ius cogens) → void; neither party can rely on it; an unregistered secret treaty can moreover not be invoked before any UN organ (Art 102(2) Charter).
Memorise: Art 53 VCLT (void at conclusion) · Art 64 (new ius cogens terminates) · Art 71 · no derogation, no persistent objector · aggression, genocide, slavery, torture, apartheid.

cards.q: Distinguish obligations erga omnes from ius cogens. State Tarsia commits genocide against a minority on its own territory. May State Uldonia, none of whose nationals are affected, invoke Tarsia's international responsibility? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Ius cogens concerns rank (non-derogability, invalidity of conflicting rules), erga omnes concerns to whom an obligation is owed (standing of all states); the prohibition of genocide is both, so Uldonia may invoke Tarsia's responsibility.
• Erga omnes (Barcelona Traction, ICJ 1970): obligations towards the international community as a whole; given the importance of the rights involved, all states have a legal interest in their protection — e.g. outlawing aggression and genocide, protection from slavery and racial discrimination. Erga omnes partes: owed to all parties of a treaty (Torture Convention — Belgium v Senegal 2012; Genocide Convention — The Gambia v Myanmar 2022).
• Ius cogens (Art 53 VCLT): norms from which no derogation is permitted → conflicting treaties void.
• Relationship: every peremptory norm gives rise to erga omnes obligations, but not every erga omnes obligation is necessarily ius cogens.
• Application: Uldonia is not an injured state (Art 42 ARSIWA), but it may invoke responsibility for the breach of an obligation owed to the international community as a whole (Art 48(1)(b) ARSIWA) and claim cessation, assurances of non-repetition and reparation in the interest of the victims (Art 48(2)). As a party to the Genocide Convention it could also bring a case to the ICJ under Art IX (as The Gambia did).
Memorise: ius cogens = rank (Art 53 VCLT) · erga omnes = standing (Barcelona Traction 1970, Art 48 ARSIWA) · all ius cogens is erga omnes, not vice versa.

cards.q: Do you agree with the following statement? Give reasons. "Soft law, such as declarations of the UN General Assembly, has no legal relevance whatsoever because it is not binding." (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No — soft law is not binding and not a source of law, but it is legally relevant as a forerunner of treaties, as evidence of opinio iuris and as an aid to interpretation.
• Definition: instruments with normative content but without binding force — non-binding resolutions and declarations of IOs (UDHR 1948, Friendly Relations Declaration 1970, Rio Declaration 1992), political declarations (Helsinki Final Act 1975), codes of conduct, guidelines, standards. They lie below the "normative threshold".
• Relevance: (1) catalyst for treaties — the UDHR led to the ICCPR and ICESCR 1966; (2) evidence of opinio iuris and crystallisation of custom — Nicaragua 1986 (Res 2625), Nuclear Weapons AO 1996 (depending on content and voting); parts of the UDHR are regarded as customary law; (3) interpretation and guidance — members must consider recommendations in good faith, conduct in conformity enjoys a presumption of legality; (4) political cost of disregarding it.
• Limit: breaching soft law as such is not an internationally wrongful act and entails no state responsibility.
Memorise: soft law = no source, not binding · but → treaties · → evidence of custom (Nicaragua, Nuclear Weapons AO) · → interpretation · no responsibility for breach.

cards.q: (June 2025 exam) Why does international law not only have written legal sources such as treaties, but also unwritten sources? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Because in a horizontal order without a legislator treaties bind only their parties and cannot regulate everything, so unwritten sources supply general law binding on all states and fill gaps.
• No central legislator: states make the law themselves; there is no world parliament that could enact written law for all. Law therefore also arises from state conduct — custom rests on tacit, general consent.
• Treaties bind only their parties (pacta tertiis, Art 34 VCLT) and universal participation is rare; custom binds all states, including non-parties and new states (except persistent objectors) — e.g. state immunity, prohibition of force (Nicaragua 1986).
• Gaps: general principles of law (good faith, estoppel, res judicata, reparation) allow a court to decide instead of declaring a non liquet.
• Foundation and flexibility: even pacta sunt servanda cannot rest on a treaty alone; custom adapts to new developments without formal amendment (outer space after 1957).
Memorise: no legislator · treaties bind only parties (Art 34 VCLT) · custom = general law for all · GPL = gap filling, no non liquet.

cards.q: Your friend says: "International law is not really law. There is no world parliament, no compulsory court and no world police, so states can simply ignore it without consequences." How would you respond? Explain the structure of the international legal order and how it is enforced. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: International law is law, but a horizontal order of coordination: its addressees create, interpret and enforce it themselves, and compliance is secured by reciprocity, self-help and collective mechanisms rather than by a central executive.
• Austin's command theory denies legal character because there is no sovereign issuing sanctioned commands. Answer: law does not require centralised enforcement; states are both authors and addressees (consent), there is a basic consensus on the validity of the order, and compliance usually pays (reciprocity, reputation) — most rules are observed most of the time.
• Decentralised enforcement: retorsion — lawful but unfriendly acts (breaking off diplomatic relations, stopping aid); countermeasures — acts that would otherwise be unlawful but are justified by the other state's prior breach (proportionate, non-forcible, respecting human rights and ius cogens, Arts 49–54 ARSIWA); self-defence (Art 51 Charter).
• Collective and institutional enforcement: Security Council measures under Chapter VII (Arts 41, 42), exclusion from IOs, international courts where consent exists, non-recognition of unlawful situations, individual criminal responsibility (ICC).
• Domestic costs: breaches strengthen the opposition, provoke interest groups, media and NGOs.
Memorise: horizontal order · consent + reciprocity · retorsion (lawful) vs countermeasure (unlawful but justified) · SC Chapter VII · ICC.

cards.q: (April 2024 exam) State Willunia has dissolved; the new small State Selenur is one of its successor states. Selenur announces that it does not accept sovereign immunity and that its courts will hear claims against foreign states even for acts performed in the exercise of sovereign authority. The President of neighbouring Cornistan replies: "Sovereign immunity is part of customary international law. It is based on a strong sense of legal obligation of the community of states." What does "sense of legal obligation" mean? How can a state express it? What is the second constitutive element of customary international law? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: "Sense of legal obligation" is opinio iuris — the acceptance of a practice as law; the second element is a general state practice.
• Art 38(1)(b) ICJ Statute: custom = "a general practice accepted as law"; both elements must be ascertained separately (ILC Conclusions on identification of custom 2018, Concl. 2).
• Opinio iuris (sive necessitatis): the practice is undertaken with a sense of legal right or obligation — in the belief that it is rendered obligatory by a rule of law (North Sea Continental Shelf 1969). It separates custom from mere usage, courtesy or habit.
• Forms of evidence (ILC Concl. 10): public statements on behalf of the state, official publications, government legal opinions, diplomatic correspondence (such as Cornistan's note), decisions of national courts, treaty provisions, conduct in connection with IO resolutions; also failure to react over time where a reaction was called for.
• Second element — state practice (ILC Concl. 6): physical and verbal acts, in some cases inaction: diplomatic acts, legislation, executive and administrative acts, decisions of national courts (e.g. courts granting immunity to foreign states), conduct in connection with treaties and resolutions. It must be general: widespread, representative and consistent.
• For immunity both elements are present (confirmed in Germany v Italy, ICJ 2012).
Memorise: custom = practice (objective) + opinio iuris (subjective) · Art 38(1)(b) · ILC 2018 Concl. 2, 6, 10 · accepted as law ≠ courtesy.

cards.q: (April 2024 exam) Selenur, a new state that emerged from the dissolution of Willunia, refuses to grant foreign states immunity for sovereign acts. It argues: "Since the founding of our state our government has criticised sovereign immunity. Therefore Selenur is a persistent objector and not bound by it." What can a persistent objector achieve with its protest? What must a state do to be a persistent objector? Can Selenur be a persistent objector? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: A persistent objector is exempted from a new customary rule if it objected clearly and consistently while the rule was forming; Selenur cannot be one, because sovereign immunity was firmly established long before Selenur came into existence.
• Effect (ILC Concl. 15(1); Anglo-Norwegian Fisheries, ICJ 1951 — the ten-mile rule "would appear to be inapplicable as against Norway inasmuch as she has always opposed any attempt to apply it to the Norwegian coast"): the rule comes into existence for all other states, but is not opposable to the objector as long as it maintains its objection. The objector cannot prevent the rule, only its own bindingness.
• Conditions (ILC Concl. 15(2)): (1) objection during the formation of the rule, before it crystallises; (2) clearly expressed and made known to other states; (3) maintained persistently and consistently. (4) Not possible against ius cogens.
• Application: sovereign immunity (par in parem non habet imperium) has been customary law for well over a century (confirmed in Germany v Italy, ICJ 2012). Selenur appeared only after the rule was established. A new state enters the existing legal order and is bound by general custom in force at the time of its birth — there is no "clean slate" for general custom. An objection "since its founding" is therefore too late: Selenur is at most a subsequent objector.
• Consequence: Selenur remains bound; if its courts assert jurisdiction over foreign states for acta iure imperii, it commits an internationally wrongful act. Its protest could only start a change of the rule if many states followed it and accepted the new position as law.
Memorise: PO = during formation + clear + made known + consistent · effect: rule not opposable to the PO only · Anglo-Norwegian Fisheries 1951 · not against established custom, not for new states, not against ius cogens.

cards.q: (April 2024 exam) The new State Selenur argues: "Sovereign immunity cannot be customary law, because not all states were actively involved in creating it. The consent of states is the pillar of the international legal order, so all states must participate in creating a rule of customary law." Do all states have to participate in creating a norm of customary international law? What else does the requirement of "generality of practice" mean? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No — custom requires general, not universal practice; states that did not participate are bound through their tacit consent unless they are persistent objectors.
• Generality is not unanimity: the practice must be sufficiently widespread and representative, as well as consistent (ILC Concl. 8). Representative = different regions, legal systems and interests; the practice of specially affected states must be included — practice must be "extensive and virtually uniform", including that of states whose interests are specially affected (North Sea 1969).
• Consistency: a "constant and uniform usage" (Asylum 1950), but not perfect conformity — it suffices that conduct is in general consistent and deviations are treated as breaches (Nicaragua 1986).
• No particular duration is required (North Sea; ILC Concl. 8(2)).
• Consent in custom is tacit and general: a state that does not object while a rule forms is taken to accept it (acquiescence); the only way out is persistent objection. New states are bound by existing custom — otherwise every new state could veto general international law.
• Application: immunity practice (national courts, immunity statutes, the 2004 UN Convention, diplomatic statements) is widespread, representative and consistent → customary law binding on Selenur.
Memorise: generality = widespread + representative + consistent (ILC Concl. 8) ≠ unanimity · specially affected states · tacit consent · persistent objection = only exit.

cards.q: State Velmora argues before an international tribunal that a customary rule obliges states to notify neighbouring states before holding large military exercises within 50 km of their border. As evidence it submits: (1) 60 bilateral treaties containing such a notification clause; (2) a General Assembly resolution "recognising" the duty, adopted by 95 votes to 40 with 50 abstentions; (3) the fact that its own armed forces and those of 30 other states regularly give such notice; (4) statements by several of these states that they notify "as a matter of courtesy and good neighbourliness". Assess the evidentiary value of each item. (5 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: None of the items proves the rule; Velmora must show a general practice accepted as law, and its evidence shows at most an emerging practice, partly expressly without opinio iuris.
• Method: both elements separately (ILC 2018 Concl. 2, 3) — general practice (widespread, representative, consistent, including specially affected states, here states with land borders and armed forces) plus acceptance as law.
• (1) Treaties (Concl. 11): a treaty rule may codify, crystallise or generate custom, and many similar treaties can be evidence. But they may equally show that states think a treaty is needed because no general rule exists; and conduct of parties performing their treaty obligations shows no opinio iuris for custom (North Sea 1969).
• (2) GA resolution (Concl. 12; Nuclear Weapons AO 1996, paras 70–71): not binding and cannot itself create custom; it may evidence opinio iuris depending on its content and the conditions of adoption. With 40 votes against and 50 abstentions general acceptance is clearly lacking → weak evidence.
• (3) Practice of 31 states: relevant physical practice (Concl. 6), but 31 of 193 states is neither widespread nor representative, especially if other specially affected states act differently.
• (4) Courtesy statements: an express denial of opinio iuris — conduct out of comity or good neighbourliness is usage, not custom (North Sea; Concl. 9(2)); this practice cannot be counted.
• Conclusion: no general customary rule (yet); at most a rule in statu nascendi, or a particular custom among those states that accept it as law (Concl. 16).
Memorise: prove both elements separately · treaties can reflect custom OR show its absence · GA resolution: content + voting (Nuclear Weapons AO) · courtesy ≠ opinio iuris.

cards.q: Human rights organisations report that more than 100 states practise torture in their prisons. State Drevia, accused of torture before the UN Human Rights Council, denies that any torture has taken place in its prisons, but adds: "Given such widespread practice, the prohibition of torture can in any case no longer be a rule of customary international law." Assess Drevia's argument. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The argument fails — widespread violations do not destroy a customary rule when states deny or justify their conduct; Drevia's own denial confirms the rule, which is moreover ius cogens.
• Nicaragua (ICJ 1986, para 186): perfect consistency is not required; it suffices that state conduct is in general consistent with the rule and that inconsistent conduct is generally treated as a breach of the rule, not as recognition of a new rule. If a state acts prima facie incompatibly with a rule but defends itself by denying the facts or invoking exceptions or justifications contained within the rule, this confirms rather than weakens the rule.
• Practice includes verbal acts: no state claims a right to torture; states conceal and deny it. Opinio iuris is overwhelming (Art 5 UDHR, Art 7 ICCPR, Convention against Torture 1984, national criminal laws).
• Application: Drevia itself denies torture and thereby acknowledges the prohibition; secret torture is not practice accepted as law but a series of breaches.
• In addition, the prohibition of torture is ius cogens (Belgium v Senegal 2012): it can be modified only by a new peremptory norm (Art 53 VCLT), and no persistent objector is possible.
Memorise: Nicaragua para 186 · deviations = breaches, not a new rule · denial or justification confirms the rule · torture ban = ius cogens.

cards.q: In a series of General Assembly resolutions and national statements, 120 states declare that placing nuclear-powered satellites in low Earth orbit is prohibited by customary international law. The only six states that actually operate such satellites have consistently rejected this view from the beginning and continue to launch them. Has a customary rule prohibiting such satellites emerged? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Probably not — practice must be extensive and virtually uniform, including the practice of specially affected states, and precisely those states act against and reject the alleged rule.
• North Sea Continental Shelf (1969): state practice, including that of states whose interests are specially affected, must be extensive and virtually uniform and must show a general recognition that a rule of law is involved. ILC (Concl. 8, commentary): the participation of states particularly involved in the activity is an indispensable factor in assessing generality — "specially affected" refers to involvement, not to power.
• Application: the statements of the 120 states are verbal practice and evidence of their opinio iuris, but they are not engaged in the activity; the only states whose conduct is materially relevant consistently act contrary to the rule and deny it. The practice is therefore not virtually uniform.
• Even if a rule emerged among the others, the six states' clear, consistent objections during its formation would make them persistent objectors (ILC Concl. 15).
• Alternative: the majority could conclude a treaty — binding only its parties (Art 34 VCLT).
Memorise: North Sea: extensive + virtually uniform + specially affected states · a headcount is not generality · objectors during formation = persistent objectors.

cards.q: Do you agree with the following statement? Give reasons. "A rule of customary international law can only arise after state practice has existed for a very long time — at least several decades." (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No — no particular duration is required; custom can form quickly if the practice is extensive, virtually uniform and accepted as law.
• North Sea Continental Shelf (1969): the passage of only a short period of time is not necessarily a bar to the formation of a new rule, provided that state practice, including that of specially affected states, was extensive and virtually uniform; ILC Concl. 8(2): no particular duration is required.
• Examples: after the Truman Proclamation 1945 continental shelf claims spread within a few years; after Sputnik 1957 satellite overflights met no protest, and the freedom of outer space followed almost at once (GA Res 1721 (1961), 1962 (1963), Outer Space Treaty 1967).
• Duration is evidence of a settled practice, not a condition. "Instant custom" based on resolutions alone, without any practice (Bin Cheng), is not accepted by the mainstream.
Memorise: no minimum duration (North Sea; ILC Concl. 8(2)) · Truman 1945, Sputnik 1957 · instant custom without practice = rejected.

cards.q: For more than 150 years, residents, officials and goods of State Pellaria have crossed a strip of State Quintara's territory to reach a Pellarian enclave. Quintara never required authorisation for civilians and goods, but Pellarian soldiers and weapons always needed Quintara's specific permission. After political tensions Quintara closes the route completely. Pellaria claims a customary right of passage. Can a customary rule exist between only two states, and what would Pellaria's right cover? Compare this with a claim to a regional custom among Latin American states. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes — a local (bilateral) custom can exist (Right of Passage 1960); Pellaria has a right of passage for private persons, officials and goods, but not for armed forces and weapons, whose passage was always based on permission rather than on a right.
• Particular custom (ILC Concl. 16): a rule applying only among a limited number of states — regional, local or bilateral — requires a general practice among the states concerned that is accepted by EACH of them as law. Stricter than general custom: the party invoking it must prove the other state's acceptance.
• Right of Passage over Indian Territory (Portugal v India, ICJ 1960): there is no reason why a local custom cannot be established between only two states; long-continued practice concerning private persons, civil officials and goods was accepted as law → a right of passage; for armed forces, armed police and arms, passage always required India's permission → no right.
• Application: Quintara's total closure violates Pellaria's customary right as regards civilians, officials and goods; refusing passage to soldiers and weapons is lawful.
• Asylum (Colombia v Peru, ICJ 1950): regional custom is possible, but the party relying on it must prove that it has become binding on the other party. Colombia failed: the practice of diplomatic asylum showed so much uncertainty, contradiction and political expediency that no "constant and uniform usage accepted as law" existed; moreover Peru had repudiated the alleged rule by not ratifying the Montevideo Conventions of 1933 and 1939.
Memorise: particular custom = practice + acceptance by EACH state concerned (ILC Concl. 16) · Right of Passage 1960 (two states suffice; civilians yes, army no) · Asylum 1950 (not proven; Peru repudiated).

cards.q: Assume that a well-established customary rule limits exclusive fishing zones to 12 nautical miles. In 1990 State Rovena proclaims an exclusive 60-mile fishing zone and arrests foreign fishing vessels there; many states protest. By 2015, 70 coastal states have proclaimed similar zones, fishing states have adapted and the protests have ceased. Was Rovena's conduct lawful in 1990? Is it lawful today? Explain the concept of a "subsequent objector" and how customary law changes. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: In 1990 Rovena, as a subsequent objector, violated the existing rule; if the new practice has since become general and accepted as law, a new customary rule has replaced the old one and Rovena's zone is lawful today.
• Subsequent objector: a state that objects to a rule after it has been established cannot escape it (unlike a persistent objector); its deviating conduct is a breach and engages its responsibility.
• Change of custom: a deviating practice can be the starting point of a new rule if other states follow it with opinio iuris and the rest acquiesce instead of protesting — the old rule is modified or replaced. Anglo-Norwegian Fisheries (1951): Norway's straight-baseline system was opposable to the UK owing to its notoriety, the general toleration of the international community and the UK's prolonged abstention from protest.
• Real-world illustration: the exclusive economic zone grew out of claims (Latin American 200-mile claims from 1947) that initially departed from the freedom of the high seas and became custom (Libya/Malta, ICJ 1985).
• Application: 1990 — breach; the arrests were unlawful and flag states could claim reparation. Today — practice of 70 coastal states, accepted by fishing states and without protest → new custom; only states that objected persistently throughout its formation could still be exempt.
Memorise: subsequent objector = too late → breach · breach + followers + acquiescence → new custom · Anglo-Norwegian Fisheries 1951 · EEZ (Libya/Malta 1985).

cards.q: Explain the relationship between customary international law and treaties. How can a treaty provision affect customary law, and can a customary rule continue to exist alongside a treaty rule with identical content? Refer to the relevant ICJ case law. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Treaty and custom are independent sources of equal rank that interact: a treaty can codify, crystallise or generate custom, and a customary rule continues to exist in parallel even where a treaty with identical content binds the parties.
• North Sea Continental Shelf (1969) — three effects: (1) codification (declaratory): the treaty restates existing custom (much of the VCLT 1969, VCDR 1961); (2) crystallisation: an emerging rule becomes custom through the negotiation and adoption of the treaty; (3) generation: a treaty rule later becomes custom through subsequent practice — requires a provision of fundamentally norm-creating character, very widespread and representative participation including specially affected states, and practice with opinio iuris. Art 6 of the 1958 Continental Shelf Convention (equidistance) met none of these → not binding on Germany, a non-party.
• Art 38 VCLT: a treaty rule may bind third states as custom — the pacta tertiis rule (Art 34) does not prevent this. Art 43 VCLT: termination of a treaty does not affect obligations a state has independently under custom.
• Nicaragua (1986): custom and treaty exist separately even with identical content; the Court applied the customary prohibitions of force and intervention because the US multilateral treaty (Vandenberg) reservation prevented it from applying the UN Charter.
• Consequences: non-parties are bound by the customary twin; withdrawal from or a reservation to the treaty does not free a state from the customary rule; later custom may also modify treaty rules.
Memorise: North Sea: codify · crystallise · generate (norm-creating + widespread incl. specially affected + practice) · Nicaragua: parallel existence · Arts 38, 43 VCLT.

cards.q: The UN General Assembly adopts a declaration stating that the intentional destruction of cultural heritage in armed conflict "is prohibited under customary international law". It is adopted by 150 votes to 5, with 10 abstentions. State Xantia, which voted against, later destroys a historic temple during an armed conflict and argues that General Assembly resolutions are not binding. Assess the legal relevance of the declaration. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Xantia is right that the resolution itself is not binding, but it can be strong evidence that a customary rule exists; if so, the rule binds Xantia regardless of its vote, unless Xantia is a persistent objector.
• GA resolutions on external matters are recommendations (Arts 10–14 Charter), not a source under Art 38, and cannot by themselves create custom (ILC Concl. 12(1)).
• They may evidence opinio iuris or reflect a rule (Concl. 12(2)): Nicaragua (1986) — opinio iuris may be deduced, with all due caution, from states' attitude towards resolutions (Res 2625); Nuclear Weapons AO (1996, para 70) — look at content and conditions of adoption (voting, wording "recognises existing law" vs "calls upon"); Chagos AO (2019) — Res 1514 (XV) declaratory of the customary right of self-determination.
• A corresponding general practice is still required (military manuals, national legislation, treaties such as the Hague Convention 1954).
• Application: 150:5:10 and declaratory wording → strong evidence of opinio iuris; with supporting practice, the prohibition is custom. A single vote against does not make Xantia a persistent objector unless it objected consistently while the rule was forming.
Memorise: GA resolution ≠ binding, ≠ source · but evidence of opinio iuris (Nicaragua; Nuclear Weapons AO para 70) · check content + voting · a vote against ≠ persistent objection.

cards.q: (February 2024 exam) The company Stardust, based in State Y, operates thousands of small satellites in Earth orbit providing cheap internet access (1,000 satellites launched in 2021, a further 1,500 in 2022). State X wants to protect its population from foreign propaganda and sends a protest note demanding that Y prohibit Stardust's activities, because the satellites over its territory violate X's territorial sovereignty. Y replies that it has been recognised under customary international law since 1957 that Earth orbit is not part of the territory of the state below. How do you assess Y's view? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Y is right — the freedom of outer space and its exclusion from state territory became customary law very quickly after Sputnik (1957) and were later codified in the Outer Space Treaty 1967, so X's territorial sovereignty argument fails.
• State territory = land, internal and territorial waters, subsoil and the airspace above (Art 1 Chicago Convention 1944). Outer space begins above the airspace; the boundary is not fixed by treaty (about 100 km in practice), and orbits lie well above it.
• Formation: after Sputnik 1 (1957) satellites overflew practically all states without protest → general practice plus opinio iuris shown by acquiescence (ILC Concl. 10(3)); a standard example of rapid custom (North Sea: no fixed duration). Whether it crystallised in 1957 or in the early 1960s is debated; by 1967 it was firmly established.
• Confirmation: GA Res 1721 (XVI) 1961 and Res 1962 (XVIII) 1963 (unanimous); Outer Space Treaty 1967, Art I (free use by all states), Art II (no national appropriation by claim of sovereignty, use or occupation).
• Application: the rule binds X as custom even without OST membership; X cannot be a persistent objector, as it objects only now. Its propaganda concern belongs under other rules (e.g. ITU broadcasting rules, non-intervention).
Memorise: territory = land + waters + airspace (Chicago 1944) · space free since Sputnik 1957 (no protest = acquiescence) · GA Res 1721/1962 · OST 1967 Arts I, II · X too late to object.

cards.q: (February 2024 exam) Stardust, a private company based in State Y, uses Earth orbit for a commercial satellite internet service. State X argues that outer space may be used only by states, not by private companies for profit. How can it be permissible under international law that outer space is used by private actors for commercial purposes? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Because no rule prohibits it (Lotus principle), a long practice of private commercial satellites has been accepted without protest, and the Outer Space Treaty itself presupposes private activities — subject to state authorisation, supervision and responsibility.
• Lotus (PCIJ 1927): what is not prohibited is permitted; X would have to prove a prohibitive rule. The freedom of use (Art I OST) is not limited to non-commercial purposes; what is prohibited is appropriation (Art II), not use.
• Practice: commercial telecommunication, broadcasting and internet satellites have operated for decades without protest → general practice accepted as law.
• Art VI OST: states bear international responsibility for national activities in outer space "whether carried on by governmental agencies or by non-governmental entities"; such activities require authorisation and continuing supervision by the appropriate state. Art VII OST and the Liability Convention 1972: the launching state is liable for damage.
• Application: Stardust's activity is lawful, but Y must authorise and supervise it and answers internationally for it.
Memorise: Lotus → no prohibition · accepted practice · Art VI OST: private activities allowed with state authorisation + supervision + responsibility · Art VII OST, Liability Convention 1972.

cards.q: What is the International Law Commission, what is its mandate, and how does its work relate to customary international law? Name two advantages and two disadvantages of codifying customary law. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The ILC is a subsidiary organ of the UN General Assembly entrusted with the codification and progressive development of international law; its drafts often become treaties or serve as authoritative evidence of custom.
• Basis: Art 13(1)(a) UN Charter (GA initiates studies and makes recommendations to encourage the progressive development of international law and its codification); established by GA Res 174 (II) 1947; 34 independent experts elected by the GA for five years, representing the principal legal systems.
• Mandate: codification = precise formulation and systematisation of existing customary law; progressive development = drafting rules on matters not yet regulated or not sufficiently developed in practice.
• Output: draft articles that became treaties (Vienna Conventions on Diplomatic Relations 1961, Consular Relations 1963, Law of Treaties 1969; UN Convention on State Immunity 2004) or remain non-binding texts (ARSIWA 2001; 2018 Conclusions on identification of custom). Non-treaty texts are not binding as such but carry great weight as evidence of custom and as a subsidiary means (Art 38(1)(d)).
• Advantages: systematisation, precision and legal certainty, progressive development, articulation of community interests, legitimisation (participation of new states).
• Disadvantages: it can freeze the law and block further development; compromise texts tend to the lowest common denominator; a failed codification leaves the customary position less certain than before.
Memorise: ILC = Art 13(1)(a) Charter, GA Res 174 (II) 1947, 34 members, 5 years · codification (existing law) vs progressive development (new law) · Vienna Conventions 1961/63/69.

cards.q: In the 1990s several states began to claim a new customary right to seize foreign cargo ships carrying hazardous waste on the high seas. From the very first claims in 1994, State Obrena protested in diplomatic notes, voted against every related General Assembly resolution and never seized a ship itself. By 2015 the new rule is accepted as custom by a large majority of states. Is Obrena bound by it? Would the answer differ (a) if the rule were ius cogens, or (b) if Obrena had itself seized such a ship in 2005? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Obrena is a persistent objector, so the new rule is not opposable to it as long as it maintains its objection; this would not work against ius cogens, and a seizure of its own in 2005 would have destroyed the persistence of its objection.
• Conditions (ILC Concl. 15; Anglo-Norwegian Fisheries 1951): objection while the rule was forming (here from the first claims), clearly expressed and made known (notes, votes), maintained persistently and consistently — all fulfilled.
• Effect: the rule exists for all other states; only Obrena escapes. Other states may not rely on the new rule to seize Obrenan ships; between them and Obrena the old rule (exclusive flag-state jurisdiction on the high seas) still applies.
• (a) Ius cogens: persistent objection does not apply to peremptory norms (ILC 2022 Conclusions on ius cogens, Concl. 14(3)) — Obrena would be bound.
• (b) Own seizure: inconsistent conduct deprives the objection of its persistent character; Obrena would be bound, at the latest from the time its conduct contradicted its objection.
Memorise: persistent objector = early + clear + made known + consistent → rule not opposable · never against ius cogens · inconsistent conduct kills the objection.

cards.q: (June 2025 exam) The land border between the neighbouring states Monturia and Lirania in a sparsely populated area has been unclear for decades; both claim a small valley containing valuable minerals. In 2022 Lirania built a mining facility there and has exploited the raw materials ever since. Monturia initially protested but took no further action. In 2025 Monturia sues Lirania before the ICJ on the basis of a bilateral treaty of friendship, arguing that the area has always been Monturian. Lirania replies that Monturia forfeited its right through its long silence and that under customary international law the area now belongs to Lirania. What is customary international law? Explain the conditions for its creation and examine whether Lirania can possibly invoke customary international law. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Customary international law is unwritten law arising from a general practice accepted as law; Lirania cannot successfully invoke it, because three years of mining against Monturia's protest create neither title by prescription nor a local custom.
• Definition: Art 38(1)(b) ICJ Statute — "international custom, as evidence of a general practice accepted as law"; binding on all states (except persistent objectors).
• Conditions, to be shown separately (ILC 2018 Concl. 2): (1) state practice — general, i.e. widespread, representative (incl. specially affected states) and consistent ("extensive and virtually uniform", North Sea 1969); no fixed duration; (2) opinio iuris — practice followed out of a sense of legal obligation or right, not courtesy or habit.
• General custom on territory: occupation concerns only terra nullius, and the valley is claimed by two states. Acquisitive prescription (its status is itself contested) would require long, peaceful, public and uninterrupted display of sovereignty acquiesced in by the other state → 3 years is far too short and Monturia protested. Acts after the dispute crystallised (the critical date) cannot improve a party's position anyway (Pulau Ligitan/Sipadan 2002).
• Local custom (Right of Passage 1960; ILC Concl. 16): would need long practice accepted as law by BOTH states — Monturia's protest shows the opposite.
• Result: Lirania's customary-law argument fails.
Memorise: custom = practice (widespread, representative, consistent) + opinio iuris · 3 years + protest = no prescription, no local custom · critical date.

cards.topic: General Principles of Law, Unilateral Acts and Subsidiary Means
cards.q: (June 2025 exam) The border between Monturia and Lirania has been unclear for decades, and both claim a small valley with valuable minerals. Lirania built a mining facility there in 2022 and has exploited the minerals ever since. Monturia initially protested but took no further action; in 2025 it sued Lirania before the ICJ on the basis of a bilateral treaty of friendship. Lirania argues that Monturia forfeited its right through its long silence. Monturia also demands compensation for the minerals extracted since 2022 plus default interest; Lirania counters that the claims are time-barred and that there is no obligation to pay interest because no treaty provides for it. What is meant by "general principles of law" in international law? Give three examples and briefly explain whether they could play a role in the dispute. (5 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: General principles of law (Art 38(1)(c) ICJ Statute) are unwritten principles common to the principal legal systems or formed within international law that fill gaps; acquiescence, prescription and full reparation including interest are all relevant — and none of them helps Lirania.
• Meaning: an independent source, not created by the will of states like treaties and custom; two categories (ILC): derived from national legal systems (common to the principal legal systems and transposable to international law) and formed within the international legal system (e.g. uti possidetis iuris). Function: gap filling, avoiding a non liquet. Examples: good faith, estoppel, acquiescence, prescription, res judicata, nemo iudex in causa sua, reparation.
• (1) Acquiescence / estoppel (good faith): silence counts as consent where a reaction was called for — qui tacet consentire videtur si loqui debuisset ac potuisset (Temple of Preah Vihear 1962; Gulf of Maine 1984). But Monturia protested, and a protest preserves its position and excludes acquiescence; three years without repetition is no "long silence", and the lawsuit maintains the claim. No estoppel either: Monturia made no representation on which Lirania relied.
• (2) Prescription: extinctive prescription (time bar) has no fixed limit; only unreasonable delay that prejudices the respondent makes a claim inadmissible (Certain Phosphate Lands in Nauru 1992) → suing after three years is timely. Acquisitive prescription of territory would need long, peaceful, uncontested possession → not met.
• (3) Full reparation including interest: every breach of an engagement involves an obligation to make reparation that wipes out its consequences (Chorzów Factory, PCIJ 1927/1928). If the valley is Monturian, the extraction violates its territorial sovereignty → compensation for the value of the minerals (Art 36 ARSIWA) plus interest from the date due until payment (Art 38 ARSIWA). Interest is part of full reparation and needs no treaty basis.
• Also relevant: nemo iudex in causa sua (Lirania cannot decide the dispute itself), res judicata (the judgment binds both, Arts 59, 60 Statute), uti possidetis iuris (if both emerged from decolonisation, the former administrative boundary decides; Frontier Dispute 1986).
Memorise: GPL = Art 38(1)(c), 2 categories, gap filling · protest excludes acquiescence (Temple a contrario) · no fixed time bar, only unreasonable delay (Nauru 1992) · reparation + interest (Chorzów; Arts 36, 38 ARSIWA).

cards.topic: General Principles of Law, Unilateral Acts and Subsidiary Means
cards.q: What is meant by "general principles of law" within the meaning of Article 38(1)(c) of the ICJ Statute? Explain the two categories identified by the International Law Commission, how such principles are identified, and their function in the system of sources. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: General principles of law are an unwritten source consisting of principles common to the principal legal systems of the world (transposed to international law) or formed within the international legal system; their main function is to fill gaps.
• Nature: unlike treaties and custom, not created by the will of states — hence their uneasy place in a consent-based system. "Recognised by civilized nations" is an outdated formula, read today as "the principal legal systems of the world" / "the community of nations".
• Category 1 — derived from national legal systems (ILC Draft Conclusions on GPL, Special Rapporteur Vázquez-Bermúdez): two steps — (a) a principle common to the various legal systems of the world, shown by a wide and representative comparative analysis covering different regions and legal families; (b) its transposition to the international legal system (compatible with its fundamental principles). Examples: good faith, estoppel, res judicata, unjust enrichment, abuse of rights, reparation for harm, interest for late payment, force majeure.
• Category 2 — formed within the international legal system: principles recognised as intrinsic to the international legal system itself, e.g. uti possidetis iuris (Frontier Dispute 1986), "elementary considerations of humanity" (Corfu Channel 1949). This category is more controversial.
• Identification: mainly the comparative method; some argue for a natural-law approach.
• Function: gap filling so that no non liquet is declared; interpretation of treaties and custom; procedural rules for international courts; internal law of IOs (staff tribunals, e.g. EPO cases); EU law (Art 340(2) TFEU, Art 6(3) TEU).
Memorise: Art 38(1)(c) · 2 categories: from national systems (common + transposition) / formed within international law · comparative method · function: gap filling, no non liquet.

cards.topic: General Principles of Law, Unilateral Acts and Subsidiary Means
cards.q: Name five general principles of law applied in international law. Explain the content of each and give an example of a case or area in which it has been applied. (5 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Examples are good faith, estoppel, res judicata, the obligation to make reparation, and the procedural principles nemo iudex in causa sua and audiatur et altera pars (further: unjust enrichment, abuse of rights, prescription, force majeure, interest for late payment).
• Good faith (bona fides): basic principle governing the creation and performance of legal obligations, whatever their source (Nuclear Tests 1974); expressed in Art 2(2) UN Charter and Art 26 VCLT (pacta sunt servanda — treaties must be performed in good faith). Basis of the binding force of unilateral declarations.
• Estoppel (venire contra factum proprium): a state cannot take a position contrary to its earlier clear representation on which another state relied to its detriment or to the advantage of the representing state (Land, Island and Maritime Frontier Dispute 1990; Temple 1962).
• Res judicata: a final judgment of a judicial body is binding between the parties and the same claim cannot be reopened (Effect of Awards of the UN Administrative Tribunal, ICJ 1954; Arts 59, 60 ICJ Statute).
• Obligation to make reparation: any breach of an engagement involves an obligation to make reparation in an adequate form, wiping out all consequences of the illegal act (Chorzów Factory, PCIJ 1927/1928; now Art 31 ARSIWA), including interest where needed (Art 38 ARSIWA).
• Nemo iudex in causa sua: no one may be judge in his own cause (PCIJ, Interpretation of the Treaty of Lausanne (Mosul) 1925) — impartiality of arbitrators and judges.
• Audiatur et altera pars: both parties must be heard and treated equally in proceedings; its violation can make an award null.
• Others: unjust enrichment (Inceysa v El Salvador), abuse of rights, extinctive prescription (Nauru 1992), force majeure (Russian Indemnity 1912).
Memorise: good faith · estoppel · res judicata · reparation (Chorzów) · nemo iudex · audiatur et altera pars · + unjust enrichment, abuse of rights, prescription, interest.

cards.topic: General Principles of Law, Unilateral Acts and Subsidiary Means
cards.q: For 30 years the government of Sarnia declared in official diplomatic notes to its neighbour Tolvia that the disputed island of Kel belonged to Tolvia. Relying on these notes, Tolvia built a lighthouse and a harbour on Kel and granted fishing licences there. Sarnia's new government now claims Kel, arguing that the notes were never approved by its parliament. Can Tolvia rely on estoppel? Distinguish estoppel from acquiescence. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes — Sarnia made clear, consistent representations on which Tolvia relied to its detriment, so Sarnia is estopped from claiming the island; acquiescence, by contrast, rests on silence and requires no detrimental reliance.
• Estoppel (general principle; venire contra factum proprium): elements — (1) a clear and unequivocal statement or representation by one state to another; (2) reliance on it by the other state to its detriment or to the advantage of the representing state (Land, Island and Maritime Frontier Dispute, ICJ Chamber 1990; North Sea 1969).
• Application: official notes by the government over 30 years = clear, consistent representation by competent organs; Tolvia invested in a lighthouse, harbour and licences = detrimental reliance → Sarnia cannot now take the opposite position. Lack of parliamentary approval is an internal matter and no excuse (cf. Art 27 VCLT); the notes may even amount to a binding recognition (a unilateral act).
• Acquiescence: tacit consent inferred from silence or inaction where the circumstances called for a reaction (Gulf of Maine 1984; Temple 1962); no representation and no detriment needed. Both rest on good faith.
Memorise: estoppel = representation + detrimental reliance · acquiescence = silence when a reaction is expected · both = good faith.

cards.topic: General Principles of Law, Unilateral Acts and Subsidiary Means
cards.q: In 1960 State Arcadia published an official map showing its border with State Borelia along a mountain ridge, placing an ancient monastery on Arcadia's side. Borelia received the map through diplomatic channels, used copies of it in its own schools and administration and never objected. In 2020 Borelia claims the monastery, arguing that it never agreed to the map line and that mere silence cannot create legal obligations. Assess the legal significance of Borelia's silence and explain what Borelia should have done. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Borelia's long silence, when a reaction was clearly called for, amounts to acquiescence in the map line; to preserve its position it should have protested in good time.
• Acquiescence (general principle based on good faith): tacit recognition shown by conduct or silence which the other party may interpret as consent (Gulf of Maine 1984) — qui tacet consentire videtur si loqui debuisset ac potuisset.
• Temple of Preah Vihear (ICJ 1962): Thailand received a map placing the temple in Cambodia, used it and did not react for decades, although the circumstances called for a reaction within a reasonable period → it had accepted the map line.
• Conditions: knowledge of the other state's claim; circumstances calling for a reaction; possibility to react; a reasonable period.
• Application: Borelia knew and even used the official map and stayed silent for 60 years → acquiescence; its claim will very likely fail.
• What Borelia should have done: protest — a unilateral act declaring that it does not accept the other state's claim as lawful. It prevents acquiescence and estoppel and preserves its position; it must be clear, timely and repeated if the other state persists.
Memorise: silence + duty to react = acquiescence (Temple 1962; Gulf of Maine 1984) · qui tacet consentire videtur si loqui debuisset ac potuisset · protest = preserves rights.

cards.topic: General Principles of Law, Unilateral Acts and Subsidiary Means
cards.q: In 1975 State Farnos expropriated factories owned by nationals of State Gilea without compensation. Gilea protested once in 1976 and then remained silent. In 2025 Gilea brings a claim for compensation before an international arbitral tribunal whose jurisdiction both states have accepted. Farnos argues that the claim is time-barred, because 50 years have passed and most of the relevant documents have since been destroyed. Is there a statute of limitations in international law? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: International law has no fixed limitation period, but extinctive prescription is a general principle: undue delay can make a claim inadmissible, which the tribunal decides in the circumstances — here Farnos has good arguments.
• Extinctive prescription (time bar) is recognised as a general principle of law (e.g. Gentini case, Italian-Venezuelan Mixed Claims Commission 1903).
• Certain Phosphate Lands in Nauru (ICJ 1992): even without a treaty provision, delay on the part of a claimant state may render a claim inadmissible; international law lays down no specific time limit; the court determines in the light of the circumstances of each case whether the passage of time renders the claim inadmissible.
• Relevant factors: length of the delay; whether the claim was notified to the respondent (keeping it alive); reasons for the delay; prejudice to the respondent's ability to defend itself (loss of evidence); conduct amounting to a waiver (which must be clear and is not presumed).
• Application: Gilea's protest in 1976 informed Farnos of the claim, which speaks against prescription; but nearly 50 years of unexplained inaction and the destruction of the relevant documents seriously prejudice Farnos's defence → the tribunal may well hold the claim inadmissible.
Memorise: no fixed limitation period · prescription = general principle (Gentini 1903) · Nauru 1992: delay may make a claim inadmissible, case by case · notice, length, reasons, prejudice.

cards.topic: General Principles of Law, Unilateral Acts and Subsidiary Means
cards.q: State Harnia unlawfully seized a cargo of oil belonging to State Idra in 2015. In 2025 an international tribunal holds Harnia responsible and awards compensation of USD 50 million for the value of the oil. Idra additionally claims interest for the ten years. Harnia argues that no treaty between the states provides for interest, and points out that Idra accepted three partial payments in 2018–2020 without ever mentioning interest. Assess. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Idra is in principle entitled to interest as part of full reparation, but by accepting partial payments without any reservation it risks being held to have waived interest on them.
• Full reparation: the breach of an engagement involves an obligation to make reparation that wipes out, as far as possible, all consequences of the illegal act (Chorzów Factory, PCIJ 1928; Art 31 ARSIWA). Compensation covers financially assessable damage including lost profits (Art 36 ARSIWA).
• Interest: payable, without any treaty basis, where necessary to ensure full reparation; it runs from the date when the principal sum should have been paid until the obligation is fulfilled, and the rate is set to achieve full reparation (Art 38 ARSIWA; interest for late payment as a general principle).
• Waiver: in the Russian Indemnity case (PCA 1912) the tribunal accepted that moratory interest was due in principle, but held that Russia had renounced it because its embassy had repeatedly accepted payments of the principal without reserving interest. A waiver must, however, be clear and is not presumed.
• Application: Harnia's "no treaty" argument fails; interest from 2015 is owed. Whether Idra waived interest depends on whether its unreserved acceptance of the partial payments clearly signalled that they settled the matter — at least for the paid amounts. Lesson: always reserve rights expressly.
Memorise: full reparation (Chorzów; Art 31 ARSIWA) · interest = Art 38 ARSIWA, from due date until payment · Russian Indemnity 1912: unreserved acceptance → waiver.

cards.topic: General Principles of Law, Unilateral Acts and Subsidiary Means
cards.q: An arbitral tribunal issued a final award in 2019 in a boundary dispute between Jorvik and Kestria, rejecting Jorvik's claims. In 2024 Jorvik starts a new arbitration with exactly the same claims. It proposes that its own deputy foreign minister act as sole arbitrator, and asks that the tribunal decide without hearing Kestria, because Kestria "already had its chance" in 2019. Which general principles of law are affected? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Jorvik's plan violates res judicata, nemo iudex in causa sua and audiatur et altera pars.
• Res judicata: a final decision of an international court or tribunal is binding between the parties; the same claim (same parties, object and legal ground) cannot be litigated again (Effect of Awards of the UN Administrative Tribunal, ICJ 1954; Arts 59, 60 ICJ Statute). Exceptions are narrow: interpretation, revision on a newly discovered decisive fact (cf. Art 61 ICJ Statute) or nullity for grave defects. → The new claim is inadmissible.
• Nemo iudex in causa sua: no one may be judge in his own cause (PCIJ, Mosul/Treaty of Lausanne AO 1925). An official of a party cannot sit as sole arbitrator — arbitrators must be independent and impartial.
• Audiatur et altera pars: each party must be heard and have an equal opportunity to present its case; a decision without hearing Kestria would be a fundamental procedural defect and a ground for nullity of the award.
Memorise: res judicata (Effect of Awards 1954; Arts 59–61 ICJ Statute) · nemo iudex (Mosul 1925) · audiatur et altera pars = right to be heard.

cards.topic: General Principles of Law, Unilateral Acts and Subsidiary Means
cards.q: State Lumeria has conducted atmospheric nuclear tests in the Pacific. After worldwide protests, Lumeria's President declares at a televised press conference, and its Foreign Minister repeats before the UN General Assembly, that "Lumeria will conduct no further atmospheric tests". A year later a new government announces new tests, arguing that press statements are political and non-binding because no treaty was concluded. Is Lumeria bound? Explain the concept and the conditions of binding unilateral declarations. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes — a public declaration by the competent organs, made in clear and specific terms with the intention to be bound, creates a legal obligation on the basis of good faith, without any treaty or acceptance (Nuclear Tests 1974).
• Concept: unilateral acts are declarations made with the intention to create, modify or terminate international rights and obligations; they are a source not listed in Art 38 ICJ Statute.
• Nuclear Tests (Australia/New Zealand v France, ICJ 1974): French statements by the President and ministers that atmospheric tests would stop were binding; no quid pro quo, acceptance or reaction of other states was required; form (oral or written) is not decisive; the basis is good faith — other states may rely on such declarations (ILC Guiding Principles 2006, GP 1).
• Conditions: (1) competent organ — heads of state and government and foreign ministers can bind the state (GP 4; Eastern Greenland 1933); (2) public declaration, which may be addressed erga omnes (GP 6); (3) intention to be bound, inferred from content and circumstances, in clear and specific terms, interpreted restrictively in case of doubt (GP 3, 7); (4) form irrelevant (GP 5); (5) not contrary to ius cogens (GP 8).
• Application: repeated public statements by the President and the Foreign Minister, specific content, in the context of international protest → intention to be bound. A change of government does not affect the state's obligations (continuity), and the declaration cannot be revoked arbitrarily (GP 10) → new tests would violate international law.
• Contrast: Frontier Dispute (Burkina Faso/Mali 1986) — a statement by Mali's head of state was not binding, as nothing indicated an intention to be bound unilaterally and the parties could have concluded an agreement.
Memorise: unilateral act = intention to be bound · good faith · competent organ + public + clear/specific · form irrelevant (Nuclear Tests 1974) · no arbitrary revocation (GP 10) · contrast Burkina Faso/Mali 1986.

cards.topic: General Principles of Law, Unilateral Acts and Subsidiary Means
cards.q: During talks in Pravia's capital, the ambassador of Oskaria asks Pravia's Foreign Minister whether Pravia will object to Oskaria extending its sovereignty over the uninhabited Morn Islands. The Foreign Minister replies orally: "Pravia will not make any difficulties in this matter." A week later Pravia's Minister of Agriculture tells journalists that Pravia "will probably also grant Oskaria fishing rights around the islands". Which of these statements bind Pravia? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The Foreign Minister's reply binds Pravia (Ihlen Declaration principle); the Agriculture Minister's vague remark to journalists does not.
• Eastern Greenland (PCIJ 1933): the oral Ihlen Declaration of 1919 by Norway's Foreign Minister ("would not make any difficulties" about Danish sovereignty over Greenland) was binding — a reply of this nature given by the Minister for Foreign Affairs on behalf of his government, in response to a request by the diplomatic representative of a foreign power, on a question within his province, binds his country.
• Application 1: identical constellation — competent organ (foreign minister, cf. ILC GP 4), acting for the government, answering a formal request of Oskaria's ambassador, on a foreign-policy matter within his competence; oral form is irrelevant → Pravia is bound not to oppose Oskaria's sovereignty over the islands.
• Other ministers may bind the state only in their own field of competence and only if specifically authorised (GP 4; Armed Activities, DRC v Rwanda 2006: a minister of justice may in certain circumstances bind the state).
