• Application 2: even if fishing falls within the Agriculture Minister's portfolio, "will probably" is not a clear and specific commitment, and in case of doubt declarations are interpreted restrictively (GP 7) → no intention to be bound, no obligation.
Memorise: Ihlen Declaration (Eastern Greenland 1933): FM + on behalf of government + answer to a foreign request + within his province = binding · other ministers only within their field (DRC v Rwanda 2006) · vague words = no obligation.

cards.topic: General Principles of Law, Unilateral Acts and Subsidiary Means
cards.q: Name and explain five types of unilateral acts of states, their legal effects and an example of each. Distinguish fully unilateral acts from unilateral acts connected with treaties. (5 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The main types are promise, recognition, protest, waiver (renunciation) and notification; fully unilateral acts operate on their own, while treaty-related acts (signature, ratification, reservations, objections) take effect within a treaty regime.
• Promise: the author assumes a new obligation towards others (Nuclear Tests 1974 — France's undertaking to stop atmospheric tests). Binding on the basis of good faith if made with the intention to be bound; cannot be revoked arbitrarily.
• Recognition: acceptance of a situation, claim or entity as legally valid — recognition of states (largely declaratory, but evidentially important) and governments, of territorial claims or borders. Effect: the author can no longer contest what it recognised (link to estoppel). Duty of non-recognition of situations created by serious breaches of ius cogens (Art 41(2) ARSIWA).
• Protest: declaration that the author does not accept another state's claim or conduct as lawful. Effect: preserves the author's legal position, prevents acquiescence and estoppel, and is the tool of the persistent objector (Anglo-Norwegian Fisheries 1951).
• Waiver / renunciation: the author gives up a right or claim (e.g. a claim to compensation). It must be clear and unequivocal and is not presumed (Nauru 1992), but may exceptionally follow from conduct (Russian Indemnity 1912).
• Notification: formal communication bringing a fact or legal act to the knowledge of other states, which then cannot claim ignorance (e.g. notification of a blockade, of withdrawal from a treaty under Arts 65, 67 VCLT, of a derogation under Art 4(3) ICCPR).
• Fully unilateral acts (the above) vs treaty-related unilateral acts: signature, ratification, accession, reservations and objections to reservations, and declarations under Art 36(2) ICJ Statute — unilateral in form, but their effects depend on the treaty framework.
Memorise: promise · recognition · protest · waiver · notification · basis = intention + good faith · treaty-related: ratification, reservation, objection, Art 36(2) declaration.

cards.topic: General Principles of Law, Unilateral Acts and Subsidiary Means
cards.q: In 2020 the Head of State of Quorra publicly declared that Quorra would supply 10,000 tonnes of grain free of charge every year to famine-stricken State Rimba "for as long as the famine lasts". In 2024, although the famine continues, Quorra announces that it is stopping the deliveries with immediate effect because it wants to export the grain. Rimba has relied on the deliveries in its food planning. May Quorra revoke its declaration? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No — a binding unilateral declaration cannot be revoked arbitrarily; since the famine continues, Rimba relied on the promise and circumstances have not fundamentally changed, the revocation is unlawful.
• Binding: public declaration by the Head of State, clear and specific, with evident intention to be bound → obligation based on good faith (Nuclear Tests 1974; ILC Guiding Principles 2006).
• ILC GP 10: such a declaration cannot be revoked arbitrarily; relevant are (a) its own terms on revocation, (b) the addressees' reliance on it, (c) any fundamental change of circumstances. Nuclear Tests: an undertaking is not made in implicit reliance on an arbitrary power of reconsideration.
• Application: the declaration fixes its own duration (the famine continues), Rimba relied on it, and an export interest is no fundamental change → Quorra remains bound; stopping deliveries is an internationally wrongful act.
Memorise: binding declaration → no arbitrary revocation (ILC GP 10) · check: terms on revocation, reliance, fundamental change.

cards.topic: General Principles of Law, Unilateral Acts and Subsidiary Means
cards.q: Do you agree with the following statement? Give reasons. "Since the ICJ decided in Nicaragua (1986) that the prohibition of the use of force is customary law, this judgment is a binding precedent for all states and all future cases." Explain the role of judicial decisions and teachings in international law. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No — ICJ judgments bind only the parties in the particular case (Art 59 ICJ Statute); judicial decisions and teachings are subsidiary means for determining the law, not sources, although a consistent case law carries great persuasive authority.
• Art 38(1)(d) ICJ Statute: judicial decisions and the teachings of the most highly qualified publicists are "subsidiary means for the determination of rules of law", expressly "subject to Art 59": the decision has no binding force except between the parties and in respect of that particular case → no stare decisis.
• ILC (Draft Conclusion 7, 2024): decisions may be followed on points of law addressing the same or similar issues, but they are not legally binding precedent unless an instrument provides otherwise.
• Practical weight: jurisprudence constante — a consistent line of decisions develops a common legal opinion (SGS v Philippines); the ICJ regularly follows its own case law; adopted WTO reports create legitimate expectations (Japan – Alcoholic Beverages).
• Teachings: highly qualified scholars and learned bodies (ILC, Institut de Droit International, International Law Association). Their weight depends on representativeness, quality of reasoning, expertise, level of agreement, reception by states and any mandate (ILC Draft Conclusion 3).
• Application: the prohibition of force binds all states because it is custom (and Art 2(4) Charter); Nicaragua evidences this rule but does not create it.
Memorise: Art 38(1)(d) + Art 59 = no stare decisis · jurisprudence constante = persuasive · the rule binds because it is custom — the judgment only evidences it.

cards.q: (June 2024 exam) The neighbouring states Rachastan and Antrania have been in conflict over the region of Bethania since their independence 45 years ago. Before independence their joint colonial power assigned Bethania to Antrania, although over 90 % of its inhabitants are ethnic Rachastanis. The states have already fought three wars over the region, and after the assassination of an Antranian politician in Bethania a new war threatens. The Foreign Minister of a third state, the St. Petersburg Federation, wants to help the parties reach a peaceful settlement. What options do third parties (non-disputing states) have to support the parties in reaching an agreement? Explain the different procedures and the role the third party plays in each. (8 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Third parties can offer the diplomatic means listed in Art 33 UN Charter — good offices, inquiry, mediation and conciliation — each with an increasing degree of third-party involvement; all require the consent of both Rachastan and Antrania, and none produces a binding result.
• Framework: Art 2(3) UN Charter (also custom, Friendly Relations Declaration 1970): disputes must be settled by peaceful means. Art 33(1): the parties shall seek a solution by negotiation, enquiry, mediation, conciliation, arbitration, judicial settlement, regional agencies or other peaceful means of their own choice. Consensualism and free choice of means: a third party can only offer its services; both parties must accept the procedure and the person. Negotiation itself is purely bilateral — no third party.
• 1. Good offices: the third party does not influence the content of the settlement; it provides the framework — neutral venue, communication channels (passing messages where relations are broken off), logistics and secretariat — so that the parties start or continue negotiating without losing face. Typical providers: neutral states and host states of IOs (Vienna, Iran nuclear deal 2015), the UN Secretary-General. Here: the St. Petersburg Federation could host talks.
• 2. Inquiry (fact-finding): a commission, usually composed with parity and working under agreed rules, clarifies disputed facts in a report. It draws no legal conclusions, its findings are not binding, and the parties draw their own conclusions (Hague Conventions 1899/1907; Dogger Bank 1904). Here: establishing the facts of the assassination could defuse the immediate trigger of war.
• 3. Mediation: the third party takes an active part and proposes terms of settlement, which are not legally binding; it may exert influence, create incentives (aid, guarantees) and work confidentially (Algeria between Iran and the US 1980–81; the US between Angola, Cuba and South Africa 1988). Here: proposals such as autonomy for Bethania, minority guarantees or a referendum.
• 4. Conciliation: a formalised, institutionalised combination of inquiry and mediation — a commission examines the facts (and law), hears the parties and submits a non-binding report proposing a compromise (Jan Mayen 1981; Timor-Leste/Australia 2016–18 under UNCLOS Annex V).
• 5. Institutional third parties: UN Secretary-General (good offices; Art 99), Security Council (may investigate, Art 34; recommend procedures or terms of settlement, Arts 36–37 — only recommendations under Chapter VI; binding measures only under Chapter VII after a determination under Art 39), General Assembly (Arts 11, 14), regional organisations (Art 52).
• Contrast: in arbitration and judicial settlement the third party decides the dispute bindingly on the basis of law — also only with the consent of both parties.
• Assessment: the third party moves from facilitator (good offices) to fact-finder (inquiry), active proposer (mediation) and formal commission (conciliation); the parties keep control over the outcome, which suits a politically charged territorial and self-determination dispute like Bethania.
Memorise: Art 2(3) + Art 33 · menu, free choice, consent · negotiation (no third party) → good offices (framework) → inquiry (facts) → mediation (proposals) → conciliation (formal commission: facts + proposals) · all non-binding · arbitration/ICJ = binding.

cards.q: (June 2024 exam) Rachastan and Antrania are in a long-standing territorial dispute over the region of Bethania. Both reject a third state's offer of mediation. Rachastan is still interested in a peaceful solution and wants the conflict resolved bindingly by an independent, impartial institution. Which procedures can Rachastan use, and what requirement must be met for them to take place? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Arbitration or judicial settlement, in particular before the ICJ; both require that Antrania also consents, because there is no compulsory jurisdiction in international law.
• Legal means: an independent third party decides on the basis of international law with binding effect — arbitration (ad hoc or via the Permanent Court of Arbitration) or judicial settlement (ICJ, Art 92 Charter; binding judgment, Art 59 Statute, Art 94(1) Charter).
• Requirement — consent of both parties, through: a special agreement (compromis); a compromissory clause in a treaty in force between them; optional clause declarations of both under Art 36(2) ICJ Statute; or forum prorogatum (Antrania accepts after Rachastan's application).
• Without consent Rachastan can only take the dispute to the Security Council or General Assembly (Art 35 Charter), which merely recommend (Chapter VI).
Memorise: binding = arbitration / ICJ · always consent of BOTH · compromis · compromissory clause · Art 36(2) · forum prorogatum.

cards.q: Do you agree with the following statements? Give reasons. (a) "Under the UN Charter states are obliged to submit every international dispute to the International Court of Justice." (b) "Article 33 UN Charter lists the methods of dispute settlement in order of priority, so negotiation must always be tried before arbitration." (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Both statements are wrong — states must settle disputes peacefully, but they are free to choose the method, and ICJ jurisdiction always depends on consent.
• Art 2(3) UN Charter: all members shall settle their international disputes by peaceful means in such a manner that international peace and security, and justice, are not endangered — also customary law (Friendly Relations Declaration 1970; Manila Declaration 1982); the counterpart of the prohibition of force (Art 2(4)).
• (a) Wrong: it is an obligation to use peaceful means and to seek a settlement, not to reach one, and not to use any particular means. There is no compulsory jurisdiction — the ICJ decides only with consent (Art 36 ICJ Statute). Art 36(3) Charter merely asks the Security Council to take into account that legal disputes should "as a general rule" be referred to the ICJ.
• (b) Wrong: under Art 33(1) the parties shall "first of all" seek a solution by negotiation, enquiry, mediation, conciliation, arbitration, judicial settlement, regional agencies "or other peaceful means of their own choice". "First of all" means before turning to the Security Council; the list is a menu, not a ranking (free choice of means). Prior negotiation is required only where a specific treaty makes it a precondition (e.g. Art 22 CERD — Georgia v Russia, ICJ 2011).
Memorise: Art 2(3) = duty of peaceful means (also custom) · Art 33 = menu, free choice, seek ≠ reach · no compulsory ICJ jurisdiction.

cards.q: Distinguish diplomatic (political) means from legal means of dispute settlement. What is a "dispute" in international law? Name advantages and disadvantages of negotiation. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: With diplomatic means the parties keep control and any result is non-binding unless they agree to it; with legal means an independent third party decides on the basis of law, and the decision is binding.
• Dispute: "a disagreement on a point of law or fact, a conflict of legal views or of interests between two persons" (Mavrommatis, PCIJ 1924); the claim of one party must be positively opposed by the other (South West Africa 1962).
• Diplomatic means — negotiation, good offices, inquiry, mediation, conciliation: flexible, confidential, may take political interests into account, not only law; outcome binding only if the parties conclude an agreement.
• Legal means — arbitration and judicial settlement: legal disputes over questions of international law; procedural and substantive law applied; binding award or judgment; require consent to jurisdiction.
• Negotiation (no third party): advantages — informality, direct contact between the parties as equals, the chance to genuinely settle (not just decide) the dispute, partnership, confidentiality; disadvantages — stalemate between equally strong parties with high stakes, and between unequal parties a solution dictated by the stronger. Where there is a duty to negotiate, negotiations must be meaningful and in good faith (North Sea 1969).
Memorise: dispute = Mavrommatis 1924 · diplomatic = parties decide, non-binding · legal = third party, law, binding, consent · negotiation: + equality, confidentiality / − stalemate, power imbalance.

cards.q: A patrol boat of State Sandoria sank a fishing trawler from State Tereno near their maritime boundary. Sandoria claims the trawler was fishing illegally in Sandorian waters and rammed the patrol boat; Tereno claims the trawler was in its own waters and was fired upon without warning. Both states want to avoid escalation but do not trust each other's evidence. Which method of peaceful settlement would you recommend, how does it work, and what is the legal value of its result? What could follow if a compromise solution is also wanted? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: An international commission of inquiry, which clarifies the disputed facts in a non-binding report; if a compromise is also wanted, conciliation (or mediation), and for a binding result arbitration or the ICJ.
• Inquiry: a third party (a commission) establishes facts only. The parties agree on its composition (usually parity plus a neutral chair), mandate and procedure; it hears witnesses, examines evidence and issues a written report. It draws no legal conclusions, its findings are not binding, and the parties may draw their own conclusions from them (Hague Conventions 1899/1907).
• Suitability: the dispute is essentially about facts (position of the trawler, ramming, warning shots). Precedents: Dogger Bank 1904 (Russian fleet firing at British trawlers — the commission's findings led to compensation), Red Crusader 1962 (UK/Denmark — the commission found the Danish vessel had exceeded legitimate use of force).
• Next steps: conciliation — a formal commission combining fact-finding with a non-binding proposal for settlement; mediation — a third party actively proposes terms; for a binding decision on responsibility and compensation — arbitration or the ICJ, with the consent of both states.
Memorise: disputed facts → inquiry (facts only, non-binding; Dogger Bank 1904, Red Crusader 1962) · + proposal → conciliation · binding → arbitration/ICJ with consent.

cards.q: Compare international arbitration with adjudication by a permanent international court. What is the Permanent Court of Arbitration, and is it a "court" in the same sense as the ICJ? Give examples. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Both are legal means leading to binding decisions based on consent, but an arbitral tribunal is constituted per case with arbitrators and law chosen by the parties, whereas a court is permanent with a fixed bench and fixed applicable law; the PCA is not a court but a permanent institution that facilitates arbitration.
• Common features: legal dispute, decision on the basis of international law, binding award or judgment, consent required (compromis/arbitration agreement, compromissory clause or general acceptance, e.g. the optional clause).
• Arbitration: tribunal constituted for each case; the parties (partly) choose the arbitrators (often one each plus a neutral president) and may determine the applicable law and procedure; confidentiality possible; the parties bear the costs. Examples: Alabama claims (US/UK, Geneva 1872), Island of Palmas (1928, sole arbitrator Max Huber), Rainbow Warrior (1990), South China Sea (Philippines v China, UNCLOS Annex VII, 2016), Iran–US Claims Tribunal (since 1981).
• Adjudication: permanently established court; the parties cannot choose the judges (only partially: judges ad hoc, Art 31 ICJ Statute; chambers, Art 26) and cannot choose the applicable law (Art 38 ICJ Statute; ex aequo et bono only if they agree, Art 38(2)); costs borne by the international community (UN budget for the ICJ). Other permanent courts: ITLOS (Hamburg, UNCLOS), regional human rights courts, CJEU.
• Permanent Court of Arbitration: created by the Hague Convention of 1899 (revised 1907), seated in the Peace Palace, The Hague; despite its name not a court — it has an International Bureau (registry) and a list of potential arbitrators nominated by member states, from which tribunals are formed for each case; it administers inter-state, investor-state and mixed arbitrations. Its national groups also nominate ICJ candidates (Art 4 ICJ Statute).
Memorise: arbitration = per case, parties choose arbitrators + law, parties pay · court = permanent, fixed bench + law, community pays · PCA 1899 = registry + list, not a real court · Alabama 1872.

cards.q: Who can be a party to contentious proceedings before the International Court of Justice, and on what bases can the Court have jurisdiction? Explain each basis with an example. (5 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Only states can be parties; the ICJ has jurisdiction only if both parties have consented — by special agreement, compromissory clause, optional clause declarations or forum prorogatum.
• Parties: only states (Art 34(1) ICJ Statute); all UN members are ipso facto parties to the Statute (Art 93(1) Charter), others under Art 93(2) Charter / Art 35(2) Statute. International organizations can only obtain advisory opinions; individuals and companies depend on diplomatic protection by their home state.
• Principle of consent: no compulsory jurisdiction; disputes about whether the Court has jurisdiction are decided by the Court itself (Art 36(6)).
• (1) Special agreement (compromis), Art 36(1) — "all cases which the parties refer to it": both states agree after the dispute has arisen (North Sea Continental Shelf 1969; Gabčíkovo-Nagymaros 1997).
• (2) Compromissory clause, Art 36(1) — "matters specially provided for in treaties and conventions in force": a treaty clause submitting disputes about its interpretation or application to the ICJ (Art IX Genocide Convention — Bosnia v Serbia 2007, The Gambia v Myanmar; Optional Protocols to the Vienna Conventions — Tehran Hostages 1980, LaGrand 2001). Limited to disputes under that treaty; any preconditions (e.g. prior negotiation) must be fulfilled.
• (3) Optional clause, Art 36(2): unilateral declarations recognising the Court's jurisdiction as compulsory "in relation to any other state accepting the same obligation" → reciprocity: jurisdiction exists only between declarant states and only as far as both declarations overlap; reservations are common. About 74 states have made such declarations (incl. Austria and the UK; the US withdrew in 1985/86 after Nicaragua).
• (4) Forum prorogatum: consent given after the application, expressly or by conclusive conduct (Corfu Channel 1948; Art 38(5) Rules of Court — Djibouti v France 2008).
• Limit: the Court cannot decide a case whose very subject-matter would be the legal interests of a third state that is not a party (Monetary Gold 1954; East Timor 1995).
Memorise: only states (Art 34) · consent · compromis + compromissory clause (Art 36(1)) · optional clause (Art 36(2), reciprocity) · forum prorogatum · Art 36(6) · Monetary Gold.

cards.q: Monturia sues Lirania before the ICJ in a dispute over a border valley. It bases jurisdiction on a bilateral treaty of friendship whose Article 20 reads: "Any dispute concerning the interpretation or application of this Treaty shall be submitted to the International Court of Justice at the request of either party." Neither state has made an optional clause declaration. Lirania objects that the friendship treaty says nothing about borders. On what basis can the Court have jurisdiction, and who decides on Lirania's objection? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Jurisdiction can rest only on the compromissory clause (Art 36(1) ICJ Statute); it covers the dispute only insofar as it concerns the interpretation or application of the friendship treaty, and the Court itself decides on Lirania's objection (Art 36(6)).
• Consent: there is no compulsory jurisdiction; a compromissory clause is consent given in advance by treaty ("matters specially provided for in treaties and conventions in force", Art 36(1)), so Monturia's unilateral application suffices.
• Scope: only disputes about that treaty. The Court checks whether the claims fall within its provisions (Oil Platforms, ICJ 1996 — Treaty of Amity). If the treaty contains e.g. a clause on respect for territorial integrity or on border resources, the claim may be covered; a pure title dispute otherwise falls outside.
• Compétence de la compétence (Art 36(6)): the Court decides, usually in a preliminary objections phase. Otherwise: special agreement or forum prorogatum.
Memorise: compromissory clause = Art 36(1) · only disputes under that treaty (Oil Platforms 1996) · Art 36(6): the Court decides.

cards.q: States Umbria and Valtia have both made declarations under Article 36(2) of the ICJ Statute. Umbria's declaration is unconditional. Valtia's declaration excludes (i) "disputes relating to the activities of Valtia's armed forces" and (ii) "disputes concerning matters which are essentially within the domestic jurisdiction of Valtia as determined by Valtia". Does the ICJ have jurisdiction if (a) Umbria sues Valtia because Valtian air defence shot down an Umbrian aircraft; (b) Valtia sues Umbria because Umbrian troops crossed into Valtia; (c) Umbria sues Valtia over a Valtian investment law, and Valtia declares the matter to be domestic? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) No and (b) no, because of the armed forces reservation, which works reciprocally; (c) probably no, if Valtia invokes its self-judging reservation — whose validity is, however, contested.
• Optional clause: jurisdiction exists only "in relation to any other state accepting the same obligation" → reciprocity: the Court has jurisdiction only to the extent that both declarations coincide, and a respondent may invoke reservations contained in the applicant's declaration (Norwegian Loans, ICJ 1957). Reciprocity concerns the scope of the obligations, not formal conditions such as notice periods (Nicaragua 1984). The Court decides on its own jurisdiction (Art 36(6)).
• (a) The shooting down is an activity of Valtia's armed forces → Valtia relies on its own reservation → no jurisdiction.
• (b) Umbria may invoke Valtia's reservation reciprocally, although its own declaration is unconditional → no jurisdiction.
• (c) Automatic ("self-judging", Connally-type) reservation: it lets Valtia itself decide what is domestic, which conflicts with Art 36(6) and arguably with good faith; some judges (Lauterpacht in Norwegian Loans) regarded such declarations as invalid, but the Court has never ruled on this and in Norwegian Loans gave effect to the reservation. Likely result: no jurisdiction once Valtia invokes it — although, objectively, a law affecting foreign investors is not essentially domestic.
• Alternatives: special agreement, a compromissory clause (e.g. in an investment treaty), forum prorogatum.
Memorise: Art 36(2) · reciprocity = only the common ground of both declarations; the respondent may use the applicant's reservations (Norwegian Loans 1957) · self-judging reservations: validity contested (Art 36(6)).

cards.q: State Wendor files an application against State Xylia at the ICJ over the treatment of Wendorian diplomats in Xylia. Neither state has made an optional clause declaration and there is no special agreement. Both are parties to the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations 1961 and its Optional Protocol concerning the Compulsory Settlement of Disputes. (a) Does the ICJ have jurisdiction? (b) Would the answer differ if Xylia were not a party to the Optional Protocol, but after receiving the application wrote to the Court that it wished to present its arguments on the merits? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) Yes, on the basis of the compromissory clause in the Optional Protocol (Art 36(1) ICJ Statute); (b) yes as well, by forum prorogatum, because Xylia consented after the application was filed.
• (a) Compromissory clause: Art 36(1) Statute covers matters "specially provided for in treaties and conventions in force". Under Art I of the Optional Protocol to the VCDR, disputes arising out of the interpretation or application of the Convention lie within the compulsory jurisdiction of the ICJ and may be brought by application of any party to the Protocol. Precedent: United States Diplomatic and Consular Staff in Tehran (ICJ 1980). The dispute concerns the treatment of diplomats, i.e. the application of the VCDR → jurisdiction.
• (b) Forum prorogatum: consent may also be given after the application is filed, expressly or by conclusive conduct (Corfu Channel 1948 — Albania's letter accepting the Court's jurisdiction); under Art 38(5) Rules of Court an application based on consent yet to be given is transmitted to the respondent, and the case proceeds only once it consents (Djibouti v France 2008). Xylia's letter is such consent → jurisdiction.
• Note: had Xylia appeared only to contest jurisdiction, this would not be consent.
Memorise: compromissory clause = treaty-based consent in advance (Optional Protocol VCDR; Tehran Hostages 1980) · forum prorogatum = consent after the application (Corfu Channel 1948; Art 38(5) Rules).

cards.q: State Yarvia wants the ICJ to state whether a wall built by its neighbour along their common border is lawful. Its Foreign Minister plans to "request an advisory opinion" from the Court directly. (a) Can Yarvia do this? (b) Who may request advisory opinions, and on which questions? (c) Are advisory opinions binding? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) No — states cannot request advisory opinions; (b) only the General Assembly and the Security Council (any legal question) and authorised UN organs and specialised agencies (questions within their scope of activities); (c) advisory opinions are not binding as such, but carry great legal authority.
• (a) A state can only bring a contentious case (which needs the neighbour's consent) or lobby the General Assembly to request an opinion — as in the Wall AO (2004), requested by GA Res ES-10/14.
• (b) Art 96(1) Charter: the GA or the SC may request an opinion on any legal question; Art 96(2): other UN organs and specialised agencies authorised by the GA may request opinions on legal questions arising within the scope of their activities (Art 65 ICJ Statute). The WHO request on nuclear weapons (1996) was rejected because the question lay outside the WHO's activities. The Court has discretion to decline for compelling reasons; the consent of the states concerned is not required, but the Court must not circumvent the principle of consent to contentious jurisdiction (Western Sahara 1975; Eastern Carelia, PCIJ 1923 — declined).
• (c) Not binding on the requesting organ or on states, but authoritative statements of the law (Reparation 1949, Namibia 1971, Wall 2004, Chagos 2019). Exception: binding where an instrument so provides, e.g. Section 30 of the 1946 General Convention on the Privileges and Immunities of the UN ("accepted as decisive" — Cumaraswamy 1999).
Memorise: Art 96 Charter: GA/SC any legal question; other organs + agencies only within their scope · states cannot request · not binding (exception: Sec. 30 General Convention) · Wall 2004, Chagos 2019.

cards.q: The ICJ orders State Zemra to pay compensation to State Aquila and to withdraw its troops from a border area. Zemra refuses, arguing that (1) the judgment is only a recommendation, (2) it was not bound by the Court's earlier order on provisional measures either, and (3) it will appeal against the judgment. Assess Zemra's arguments and explain what Aquila can do. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: All three arguments fail — ICJ judgments and provisional measures are binding, there is no appeal, and Aquila can turn to the Security Council under Art 94(2) Charter and take lawful countermeasures.
• (1) Binding force: the decision binds the parties in respect of that case (Art 59 ICJ Statute); each UN member undertakes to comply with the ICJ's decision in any case to which it is a party (Art 94(1) Charter). Non-compliance is itself an internationally wrongful act.
• (2) Provisional measures (Art 41 Statute) are binding (LaGrand, ICJ 2001) → Zemra already breached the order.
• (3) The judgment is final and without appeal (Art 60 Statute). Only: a request for interpretation if the meaning or scope is disputed (Art 60); revision (Art 61) on the discovery of a decisive new fact unknown to the Court and the requesting party, not due to negligence — within six months of discovery and at most ten years after the judgment.
• Aquila's options: recourse to the Security Council, which may, if it deems necessary, make recommendations or decide upon measures to give effect to the judgment (Art 94(2) Charter) — subject to the veto of the permanent members (the US vetoed such a draft after Nicaragua 1986); countermeasures that are proportionate and non-forcible (Arts 49–54 ARSIWA); retorsion; political pressure, including in the General Assembly.
Memorise: Art 59 (parties, this case) · Art 60 (final, no appeal; interpretation) · Art 61 (revision: new fact, 6 months / 10 years) · Art 94(1) comply, Art 94(2) Security Council (veto!) · LaGrand 2001: provisional measures binding.

cards.q: A long-running border dispute between States Borana and Castia is escalating. Borana asks the UN Security Council to "decide, with binding effect under Chapter VI of the Charter, the course of the border". Castia argues that the Security Council has no role at all as long as no war has broken out. Assess both views and explain the role of UN organs in the peaceful settlement of disputes. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Both are wrong — under Chapter VI the Security Council can already act when a dispute is likely to endanger peace (so Castia is wrong), but it can only make recommendations and cannot impose a binding border settlement (so Borana is wrong).
• Chapter VI: any member may bring a dispute to the SC or GA (Art 35); the SC may investigate (Art 34), call on the parties to settle peacefully (Art 33(2)), recommend procedures (Art 36(1); legal disputes should as a rule go to the ICJ, Art 36(3)) and recommend terms of settlement (Art 37(2)). All non-binding; parties to the dispute abstain from voting (Art 27(3)).
• Borana: a binding decision is possible only under Chapter VII after a determination under Art 39 (threat to the peace, breach, aggression); even then the SC is a political body, not a court (exceptional: Iraq–Kuwait boundary, SC Res 687 (1991), 833 (1993)).
• Castia: prevention is the very purpose of Chapter VI — the SC acts when a dispute is likely to endanger peace, not only after war breaks out.
• Other actors: GA (recommendations, Arts 11, 14, subject to Art 12); Secretary-General (good offices; Art 99); regional arrangements first for local disputes (Art 52(2), (3)).
Memorise: Chapter VI = recommendations only (Arts 33–38), parties abstain (Art 27(3)) · binding only Chapter VII (Art 39) · GA Arts 11, 14 · Secretary-General Art 99 · regional Art 52.
